articles.title: UK's rarest bird of prey rears new chicks in secret location
articles.summary: The Montagu Harrier successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location.
articles.body:
The UK's rarest bird of prey has successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) has reported.

A male Montagu's harrier, known as "AU" by conservationists, bred with two different females, rearing six chicks across two nests on English farmland.

Montagu's harriers were put on a "red list" of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021. Numbers have declined from a high of nine successful nests in 2011, to no evidence of successful breeding between 2020 and 2024.

An RSPB spokesperson said: "We are doing our absolute utmost to save this iconic species in the UK and are delighted with six flying juveniles this year."

Four chicks hatched in the same secret location last year.

The charity said careful monitoring, in partnership with the farmers on whose land the birds nested, meant the nests were protected by fences to exclude ground predators such as foxes.

The single male Montagu's harrier has also been working very hard to keep his two nests of hungry chicks fed.

The BBC was given exclusive access to the nest and was able to witness some of the spectacular feeding behaviour of the raptors: the male drops prey in mid-air and the female rolls upside down to catch it in her talons.

These slender, long-winged raptors make an epic annual migration to Africa in winter and return to Europe to nest over summer, often setting up home in agricultural fields.

But little is known about the behaviour of juvenile harriers once they leave the nest. This year, for the first time, the RSPB has fitted two of the chicks with satellite tags in the hope of providing the birds with better protection.

"It will allow us for the first time ever to work out where they're going, what migration route, how long they'll spend there, and will they come back to the UK in the first year or the second year," said Mark Thomas, head of investigations at the RSPB.

"All of that information is the bit that's missing from the jigsaw."

It is also hoped the tagging can better protect the rare birds from having their nests, on the ground, hidden among crops, inadvertently destroyed.

"This is a species right on the brink, and climate change is not helping that. The harvest here, for example, this year, was like a month earlier than in previous years. So it almost puts any Montagu's harrier nest at the peril of inadvertently being destroyed by farm machinery," said Thomas.

Conservationists have urged birders to look out for the youngsters, and report any sightings by emailing the RSPB's Montagu's hotline at montys@rspb.org.uk.

articles.title: Norway's King Harald V's health has worsened, palace says
articles.summary: Norway's King Harald remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bloodstream bacterial infection.
articles.body:
King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream.

The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice.

The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago.

His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.

King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.

In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia.

The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026.

Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018.

The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg HÃ¸iby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence.

HÃ¸iby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure.

Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

articles.title: Zolani Tete: Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
articles.summary: One of the suspects is due in court on Monday to be charged with murder and attempted murder.
articles.body:
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.

Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.

One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.

Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.

The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.

Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.

The motive behind the attack is unclear.

Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."

Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".

Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.

He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.

Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.

He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.

After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.

Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.

According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

articles.title: US firefighters say major blaze near Reno about a quarter contained
articles.summary: But officials fear that winds could fan the flames for two more days, as many locals remain under evacuation orders.
articles.body:
US fire crews have reported progress in their efforts to tackle a large wildfire menacing the city of Reno, Nevada - saying the blaze is about a quarter contained.

The Hawk Fire, which began on Saturday, had spread over 15,000 acres by Monday, firefighters said.

Evacuation orders remain in place for 23,000 people, though other residents have now been allowed to return to their homes. Tens of thousands of other residents have been told to be ready to leave at any moment.

Officials are concerned that gusts of wind could drive the flames towards more homes. Unfavourable weather conditions are forecast for the next two days, meaning the fire could continue to burn during that timeframe.

No deaths have been reported, though seven people have been injured.

The fire, which was first reported on Saturday morning, spread in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains near Reno due to those same windy and unpredictable weather conditions.

The immediate "go now" evacuation zone and wider "get set" area - where people are being warned to prepare to evacuate - do not extend to the centre of Reno, but they do affect large urban areas and part of a highway.

Large air tankers and helicopters have been flying over the affected area dropping water and fire retardants.

In their update on Monday afternoon, fire officials said the blaze had been at least 27% contained.

Chief Richard Edwards, of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said those injured were four civilians and three firefighters, who suffered minor burns.

Edwards added that 32 homes had been destroyed and six damaged, and that those numbers were expected to increase. Shelters have been set up in the area to take in displaced residents.

While firefighters have made progress, more than two-thirds of the fire's perimeter remains uncontained.

The fire is thought to have been caused by humans. Edwards added on Monday that investigators did not yet know if the blaze was set intentionally.

Scientists say that human-induced climate change makes the warm, dry conditions more likely that assist the rapid spread of wildfires.

Reno's average temperature has gone up by over 4C since the 1970s, faster than any other big US city, according to Climate Central.

Nevada's Governor Joe Lombardo earlier declared a state of emergency in surrounding Washoe County, and ordered the National Guard to join firefighting and law enforcement efforts.

"This is an active and rapidly evolving situation and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said on Saturday.

Firefighters from Australia and New Zealand have so far taken part in the containment effort â as well as crews from 15 US states.

The University of Nevada in Reno - which has its main campus in the city close to the "get set" warning area - previously said regular campus operations would continue but that it was monitoring the situation.

But one student, James Wolfgang Perez, said some teaching staff had independently decided to cancel their classes. The sight of the fire spreading in the direction of the campus on Saturday had been "apocalyptic", he told the BBC.

Justin Davis, 29, lives on Peavine Mountain, close to Reno, and similarly watched as the fire spread towards his home on Saturday and destroyed four of his vehicles.

He told the BBC he had previously bought a water truck in case a wildfire like this occurred and had used it to save his home.

"We turned on the water truck and just started spraying down the things we wanted to save," he said.

The blaze has been been named the Hawk Fire because it was first reported near the Hawk Meadow Trail, to the west of Reno.

Reno, in western Nevada, is located close to the state boundary with California and has a population of around 280,000 people.

Wildfires are common in south-western US states, including Nevada, and are becoming more severe, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Many of these fires develop in rural and less populated areas, with only a few encroaching on population centres.

articles.title: In 1934, an Arizona father began gathering rejected objects and desert Stone; 11 years later, the salvage had become an 18-room castle for his daughter
articles.summary: US News: Discover the story behind Mystery Castle in Arizona, built by Boyce Luther Gulley from discarded materials as a tribute to his daughter Mary Lou. Explore its unique architecture and historical significance.
articles.body: In the foothills of Phoenixâs South Mountain, an extraordinary house was built from materials most people would have thrown away. Between the 1930s and 1945, Boyce Luther Gulley gathered desert stone, rejected bricks, old railway materials, telephone poles, automobile parts and other discarded objects to build an 18-room castle for his daughter, Mary Lou. He worked largely by hand, shaping an eccentric three-level home into the desert landscape without a conventional architectural plan. What began as a private project became one of Phoenixâs most unusual landmarks.Today known as Mystery Castle, the structure stands as a striking example of vernacular architecture and an early exercise in material reuse. The National Trust for Historic Preservation says Gulley built the castle without formal architectural or engineering training, combining local materials, folk-art influences and recycled objects. The building eventually became a nationally recognised attraction, but its story began with a father separated from his young daughter and a promise connected to the sandcastles they had built together.From Seattle to the Arizona desertGulley was a Seattle businessman who had some training in architectural engineering. In the late 1920s, after being diagnosed with tuberculosis, he left his family and travelled to Phoenix, where the dry climate was then considered beneficial for people suffering from the disease. He eventually settled near South Mountain, at a time when the foothills were far less developed than they are today.Mary Lou had enjoyed building sandcastles with her father. The idea of creating something permanent may have stayed with Gulley after he moved west. Over the following years, he began assembling a house from whatever materials he could obtain. The National Trust dated construction of Mystery Castle to about 1934â1945. Architectural historians, however, noted that Gulley had begun building on the site earlier, with the structure evolving gradually rather than following a conventional construction plan. The result was a sprawling house that followed the contours of the hillside rather than imposing a regular architectural grid.A house assembled from what others rejectedThe castleâs unusual appearance was not simply the result of cheap materials. Gulley made the discarded objects part of the building's design. Railroad components became structural or decorative elements, old bricks became architectural details, and stones were carefully arranged into walls, fireplaces, niches and platforms.Historical Archaeology has shown that reusing building materials is not exclusively a modern sustainability idea but has long existed within vernacular building traditions. Inside Mystery Castle, practicality and eccentricity frequently overlap. The 18 rooms include a chapel, a bar and a room known as Purgatory. The building contains 13 fireplaces and a network of stairways and unusual passages. Built-in furniture was incorporated directly into the masonry, while some windows and decorative features were made from salvaged materials.The result was a building in which almost every feature carried a story about its previous life. Materials that might otherwise have been overlooked or discarded were given new functions within the castle, making the structure as much a collection of reused objects as a home. Its unconventional construction also reflected Gulleyâs determination to build according to his own ideas, without following the standard plans or materials used in conventional houses.Mary Lou inherits the castleMary Lou was 22 when she learned that her father had left her the property. She and her mother, Frances, travelled to Arizona and moved into the castle. The castle soon acquired another identity. In 1948, LIFE magazine featured Mary Lou and the unusual house in a story that helped give it the name Mystery Castle. The attention drew curious visitors, and Mary Lou and her mother later began offering tours. For decades, Mary Lou became the property's principal keeper and public guide, sharing the story of the building with visitors.Mary Lou died in 2010 after living at the castle for many decades. Before her death, she established a foundation to help preserve the property. The structure later faced another challenge. After vandalism and break-ins, Mystery Castle closed to the public in 2023, and a subsequent assessment found that stabilisation, repairs and accessibility improvements would cost about $3.3 million.In 2024, the National Trust for Historic Preservation placed Mystery Castle on its list of Americaâs 11 Most Endangered Historic Places. The designation brought renewed attention to a building whose greatest strength and weakness are closely connected: it was built as a highly individual, handmade structure rather than a conventional one designed for easy maintenance. Rejected bricks, old metal, desert rock and salvaged household materials were given new purposes and assembled into something that could not have been produced from a standard building plan. What survived was not simply a house, but an intensely personal architectural landscape built piece by piece for a daughter who would spend much of her life caring for it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: E1 settlement: Why Netanyahu, Israel’s right might not mind global outrage
articles.summary: The settlement threatens Palestinian statehood. But it could help Israel’s PM, other far-right leaders before elections.
articles.body:
The Israeli government last week invited bids for the building of more than 1,200 units, a key step towards the construction of the E1 settlement in the occupied West Bank just two months before Israel’s general election.

E1 (East 1) would link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two. Both supporters and critics agree that its construction would end the possibility of a Palestinian state.

list 1 of 4 Analysis: Israel’s government can’t disown West Bank settler violence

list 2 of 4 Palestinians, UK condemn Israel’s ‘destructive’ E1 settlement plan

list 3 of 4 Europe, Canada condemn Israeli plans for new West Bank settlement

list 4 of 4 Why Israeli tenders for illegal E1 West Bank settlement prompted outrage

The move has drawn international outrage, including from the United Nations.

But sections of Israel’s political class are using this global backlash to their own ends and could frame their support for E1 as a key pitch in their election campaigns.

Many on Israel’s right, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, thrive on the international outrage their comments and plans draw, particularly criticism from European nations.

Since October 2023, Netanyahu has cast international criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as an “us vs them” moment for the country. He has frequently framed Israel as alone in a hostile world and that he is the only leader strong enough to stand up to the country’s critics.

After the United Kingdom’s Foreign Minister Ed Miliband described E1 as an “unacceptable and destructive act”, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar criticised the “patronising tone” of his statement.

With the election approaching, the way ministers respond to the E1 project could determine their political futures.

Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has been one of the key proponents of E1 and could benefit from an uptick in support from right-wing Israelis over the proposed illegal settlement. His Religious Zionist Party is currently unlikely to pass the electoral threshold to even run in this year’s election.

“It’s Smotrich, he’s hyping up everything under his watch ahead of the election,” Israeli analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera from Berlin, Germany.

The fact that the government’s call for tenders to construct E1 falls so close to Israel’s election is not a coincidence, Flaschenberg said. Neither is the dramatic increase in settler violence in the occupied West Bank, where Smotrich has administrative control.

“Both he and even Netanyahu are benefitting from the outrage. Little of this is accidental,” the analyst added.

Condemnation of the E1 settlement has been almost universal. On Friday, the foreign ministers of Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the United Arab Emirates rejected the E1 settlement, calling for “immediate action to halt the E1 settlement plan”.

Earlier in the week, 15 European and North American leaders, including those from Israel’s traditional allies the United Kingdom, France and Germany, condemned the settlement.

In a joint letter , they said E1 would “undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank”. Some have pointed out that their failure to present any penalties if Israel goes ahead with the plan makes their criticism moot.

The United States has not criticised E1 itself, but did on Friday state its opposition to Israel’s annexation of the West Bank, which the illegal settlement could effectively result in.

“As the president has clearly stated, the US does not support Israel annexing the West Bank. A stable West Bank keeps Israel secure and is in line with this administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region,” read a statement from the US Department of State.

So, is this really the end of the two-state solution?

Announcing plans for construction in August 2025, Smotrich had boasted that the new settlement would bury the “idea of a Palestinian state”.

Given that thousands of Palestinian homes have been demolished by Israel since its occupation of the West Bank began in 1967, some hope the same could happen to the illegal Israeli settlements that replaced them, if the two-state solution becomes a reality.

“The idea that this is irreversible is just nonsense. Every time there’s a new illegal settlement, voices in the West say that this is the end of the two-state solution,” Flaschenberg said.

“It definitely makes it less likely, but why the end? Every illegal settlement that’s been built can be demolished … why do we have to accept their presence as fact?”

Political analyst Ori Goldberg noted that the tender for the E1 settlement project came at a time Israel faced further international criticism for bombing an airfield in Syria and described the issuing of the tender as “a deliberate provocation”.

Thousands of Palestinians, most of them Bedouin, have already suffered home demolitions, displacement and restrictions on basic services as Israel expands its road network before construction in the occupied West Bank.

In April 2026, 23 Palestinians, including 15 children, were displaced from the az-Za’im Bedouin community following demolitions by the Israeli army.

The UN warns that the planned expansion of Israeli illegal settlements and associated infrastructure threatens to fragment the occupied West Bank and could forcibly displace the 18 Palestinian communities that have lived within the territory Israel now claims for decades.

articles.body: Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spoke with US President Donald Trump last week, days before his planned visit to Tehran, according to three Pakistani sources cited by Reuters.The previously unreported call came as Washington prepared to impose major economic sanctions targeting Iran and countries that trade with Tehran. It remains unclear what Munir and Trump discussed.Munir is scheduled to travel to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders as Islamabad steps up efforts to revive stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran.Iran's foreign ministry announced Munir's visit on Sunday, saying he would discuss bilateral relations and regional issues with Iranian officials.He will be accompanied by a delegation expected to hold high-level meetings with the Iranian leadership.The visit comes as Pakistan seeks to revive diplomatic efforts between the United States and Iran after an interim agreement aimed at creating a 60-day window for high-level peace talks broke down last month.Pakistan had signed the agreement as a guarantor and has since been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to the negotiating table.Pakistan has increased its diplomatic engagement with Iran in recent weeks. Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi travelled to Tehran earlier this month and met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that Munir's visit would focus on strengthening bilateral cooperation and supporting efforts to promote peace and security in the region.The Pakistani government has not officially commented on Munir's reported conversation with Trump.The reported Trump-Munir call comes as Washington steps up pressure on Tehran.Trump warned on August 20 that the United States would launch what he called the âmost crushing economic operationâ against Iran if Tehran failed to reach a deal.Pezeshkian on Sunday defended the June agreement, describing it as the best way for Iran to move beyond a situation of âneither war nor peaceâ.At the same time, Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's new hard-line head of the Supreme National Security Council, warned neighbouring countries against joining any renewed US campaign targeting Iran's economy.The earlier negotiations collapsed after tensions between Washington and Tehran escalated in mid-July, following renewed military strikes.Pakistan's mediation efforts have so far failed to produce a breakthrough, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a major obstacle amid disruptions to one of the world's most important energy shipping routes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: I have eight kids. Here's why the 'back-to-school' mom memes break my heart
articles.summary: A mom of eight shares why back-to-school memes celebrating kids leaving may send the wrong message to children who notice more than we think.
articles.body: Summer is the best season. My kids have no school commitments and our time is spent getting together with friends, doing weekend trips, camping, going to the lake, and enjoying the time we have with each other. My oldest is already in college so I know the feeling of time slipping through my fingers as my kids get older and create lives of their own. Time with my husband and eight children is my most precious gift and while back-to-school season is exciting, it’s certainly bittersweet. The joy of watching my kids grow into the next stage of life is balanced out by the feeling that most of August is the Sunday before school starts. Raising kids is hard, and it’s okay to feel a little relief when structure returns. But I think we should be thoughtful about the message our children receive in the way we celebrate. JO FROST CALLS OUT MODERN PARENTING MISTAKES SHE SAYS ARE ROBBING CHILDREN OF BASIC LIFE SKILLS Scrolling through social media this time of year brings meme after meme of parents, usually moms, who are thrilled the school year is starting because it’s time to ship their kids off to someone else five days a week. The photos of moms in robes on their doorstep holding a glass of wine are everywhere. Kids notice when we seem overly eager to send them away. They remember whether we treated their presence as a burden or a gift. They hear how their parents are elated about sending them elsewhere for hours every day. Kids are much more perceptive than we give them credit for. Even if all of the back-to-school jubilation is in jest, deep down they know they are of some undue burden to their parents. NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD Conflicting emotions are common and parents shouldn’t beat themselves up over them. A study of 2,000 parents over the summer revealed 57% were happy about their kids returning to school but also felt guilty about it. Yet a different study showed 67% of parents who thought summer break was too long. I get that parents need a break, especially from the endless snack requests and demands of kids over the summer. No parent should be shamed for taking care of themselves in order to be a better parent for their kids. Yet that’s not what back-to-school season has become. It’s become a time when parents can thrillingly announce to the world that they are so happy to dump their kids at school and make them someone else’s problem. WHO IS RAISING AMERICA'S CHILDREN? MENTOR WARNS KIDS ARE SEEKING ROLE MODELS ONLINE AS COMMUNITIES FADE In a culture that has so devalued the family and children, this isn’t a surprise but it is disheartening. I used to think these kinds of posts were funny until I really thought about it. We only have so much time with our kids until they move out, go to school, and have lives of their own. I’m proud to watch my kids begin a new school year. I’m excited for what they’ll learn and who they’ll become. But I’m also sad to see summer end because I love having them home. I love the memories, the slow mornings, the time together, and the little moments that pass far too quickly. Parenting is hard and no one could ever be prepared for it, no matter how many books they read or other parents they talk to. We have so much responsibility on our plates that it can easily be overwhelming. Humans will make decisions based on their priorities — that’s what it all comes down to. Faith, marriage, kids, work, and hobbies all vie for the top spot and we have to make hard decisions every day but if those priorities are in order, it will be much easier to choose the right thing. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION I’m not suggesting every parent homeschool or drop everything to spend 24 hours a day catering to their kids. I’m saying that our children are incredible gifts and we should not be so anxious to shove them out the door and on the school bus for eight hours a day for nine or ten months of the year. Get involved in your kid’s school. Coach their rec team. Invite their friends for a movie night or ice cream or pizza making party at your house. Go on a hike with your kids and their friends. Be present. Put your phone down. Ask questions. Say ‘yes’ more. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We only have one life. Our kids are only young once and they see everything. I make plenty of mistakes as a mom but valuing the time I have with them is one mistake I try the hardest to avoid. So yes, celebrate back-to-school season. Just make sure your kids know they are loved, wanted, and deeply missed when they’re away.

articles.title: In 1900, JP Morgan bought 117 acres including Maineâs Sand Beach as a wedding gift; his granddaughter later donated about 100 acres to Acadia National Park
articles.summary: US News: In 1900, financier J P Morgan bought 117 acres in Maine, including Sand Beach and Great Head, as a wedding gift for his daughter Louisa. The land is n.
articles.body: In 1900, financier J P Morgan bought 117 acres in Maine, including Sand Beach and Great Head, as a wedding gift for his daughter Louisa. The land is now part of Acadia National Park.The land around Great Head and Sand Beach was connected to Louisa and and her husband Herbert Satterlee for decades before it became a public property. According to National Park Service, the familyâs summer property was commonly known as 'Satterlee field'.The 117 acres purchased by financier J P Morgan included Sand Beach and Great Head. Louisa married Herbert Satterlee in New York City in November 1900. The couple later made the coastal property part of their familyâs summer life.Louisa and Herbert had two daughters, Mabel, born in 1901, and Eleanor, born in 1905. The two girls grew up exploring the landscape around their familyâs property.The story of Satterlee FieldAlthough J P Morgan purchased the land in 1900, the transaction was not formally completed until 1910 because of title issues.Before the property eventually became part of the Satterlee familyâs estate, the family already had a connection with Acadia National Park because large sections of park land bordered Satterlee Field. The Satterlees also allowed park visitors to explore Sand Beach while the land was still associated with the family.The familyâs time at the summer estate came to an end after the deaths of Louisa and Herbert. Louisa died in October 1946, while Herbert died in July 1947.A few months later, the area was hit by the October Fire of 1947. Much of the Satterlee estate was destroyed in the fire. After the fire, the familyâs connection to the land changed. Eleanor and Mabel decided to donate the property so that other people could continue to visit and enjoy the landscape that had been important to their family.How family estate became public landEleanor Morgan Satterlee, Louisa and Herbertâs daughter and J P Morganâs granddaughter, inherited the tract after her parents died. By the late 1940s, Eleanorâs health had also begun to decline.These circumstances, along with the damage caused by the 1947 fire, led Eleanor to donate the land to Acadia National Park in 1949. The donation included the area around Great Head, including Sand Beach.The National Park Service records that Eleanor donated approximately 100 acres to the United States in memory of her mother, Louisa P Satterlee.A bronze plaque near the top of the staircase leading down to Sand Beach marks the donation. It carries the following inscription- âSatterlee Field, of approximately 100 acres, was donated in 1949 by Eleanor Morgan Satterlee to the United States of America in memory of her mother, Louisa P. Satterlee, as part of Acadia National Park.âThe landscape todayThe property includes the sandy beach, reached by a staircase, and the stretch of land known as the Headlands. The National Park Service describes the landscape in terms of a human body, with the coastline forming the 'shoulders' and the projecting land resembling a 'head'.The area can now be explored by visitors through the Great Head Trail. The same combination of beach, forest, mountains and coastline that the Satterlee family knew remains part of the visitor experience at Acadia.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
